```text
          This is one of the things I tell my clients. There aren’t that
      many things you can control. We can control what we eat. We
      can control how we sleep. And with mindfulness we can actu-
      ally control what we think about, and we call that focus. My
      objective is to watch every bet of every street of every hand.
      I am never able to do that but that is what I am aiming for.

   The great thing about mindfulness training is that it’s freely available to
everyone, and you can work it into spare moments of your day. Stuck in
traffic? Practice mindfulness. In a line at the grocery store? It’s a great
time to practice being mindful. Playing cards? That’s probably the best
possible opportunity to be fully present and aware of what’s going on
around you.
   If you only take one idea away from this book, I hope it is that you
start a regular mindfulness practice. It has the power to revolutionize
your mindset, because it teaches you to regulate your attention and emo-
tions. Jon Kabat-Zinn is a leader in the area of mindfulness-based stress
reduction, which is a mindfulness program used to reduce stress. He gives
a more extensive definition in Full Catastrophe Living (2009, p. 1):

      Mindfulness is awareness, cultivated by paying attention in a
      sustained and particular way: on purpose, in the present mo-
      ment, and nonjudgmentally. It is one of the many forms of
      meditation, if you think of meditation as any way in which we
      engage in 1) systematically regulating our attention and en-
      ergy, 2) thereby influencing and possibly transforming the
      quality of our experience, 3) in the service of realizing the full
      range of our humanity, and of 4) our relationship to others
      and the world.

   This is a pretty complete definition, and I’d like to call your attention to
several things. First, mindfulness is a process of awareness and not of
thinking. It involves paying attention to your experience in the present
```

```text
moment instead of being caught up in your thoughts about what’s going
on. Second, it involves an attitude of openness and curiosity. It is human
nature to try and fight negative feelings or to run away from them; being
mindful means that you do neither of those things. Instead, you are open
to what’s happening and maybe even a little curious about it. Finally,
mindfulness gives your attention flexibility. You can consciously direct
your focus to different aspects of your experience.
   An important step in developing an unbeatable mindset is to learn how
to focus where you want. At any given moment, we have many choices
about what to pay attention to. There are sights and sounds that can cap-
ture our regard, and it’s all too easy to be drawn into our thoughts and
feelings. What do you need to focus on to play your best? Conversely,
what types of things do you focus on when you slip off your A game?
   Most players play their best when they are fully focused on the pre-
sent moment. It’s hard to play your best game when your mind is focused
on a hand that has already been played or if it’s oriented on what might
happen in the future. Cultivating a present oriented, non-judgmental fo-
cus is one of the best things you can do for your game. Besides helping us
to improve our focus, mindfulness is a handy skill to cultivate because it
decreases stress, increases self-awareness, and allows us to be more in
control of our moment to moment behavior. While it’s great to have a
sense of what mindfulness is about, the only real way to learn it is to ex-
perience it first-hand. The easiest way to get started with mindfulness
meditation is to do a breathing meditation. Here’s one for you to try.
```

```text
Mindful Movement: Walking Mediation
Some people prefer a more active form of mindfulness. Luckily, there are
several to choose from. You can try yoga, tai chi, or what is known as a
walking meditation. You can try this one whenever you have a few min-
utes to walk, and it can be useful on tournament breaks. Here are the
steps:

   ♠ As you are walking, slow down and pay special attention to the
       physical sensations of walking. How do your feet feel when your
       soles meet the ground? How about when your weight transfers
       from one foot to the other?
   ♠ Now notice the flex and tension in your legs. If you become
       distracted at any time, simple redirect your attention back to the
       sensations of walking.
   ♠ You will likely find this exercise more useful if you walk slowly and
       deliberately.
   ♠ Anytime you notice your thoughts wandering, simply redirect your
       attention. Repeat as necessary.


The Body Scan
This mindfulness technique is useful because it can be very relaxing (al-
though that’s not its intended purpose) and it teaches you to become
more aware of what’s going on in your body each moment. This exercise
is an awareness practice because you are training your mind to pay close
attention to your present experience non-judgmentally. You can do the
```

```text
   ♠ Close your eyes.
   ♠ Begin by bringing your attention to the toes on your left foot.
      Notice any sensations that exist in your toes. We don’t often
      notice our toes unless they are hurt, so take this time to pay
      attention to how they feel right now, without trying to change
      anything. If you do notice that the sensations in your toes change,
      be aware of it but don’t try to change it.
   ♠ Now shift your attention to the top of your left foot. Notice how it
      feels right now. You may notice the feeling of your skin against
      your socks or sensations of temperature, tension, pressure,
      tingling, and so on.
   ♠ Each time you notice your mind wandering from the body part you
      are focused on, acknowledge that it has wandered and gently
      return it to the body. Your mind will wander as you do this
      exercise because that’s what minds do. Don’t get self-critical or
      angry about this; just return to your body scan in a non-
      judgmental way.
   ♠ Slowly progress this throughout your body. Go up your left leg to
      your pelvis. Then repeat the process on your right side starting
      with the toes on your right foot. Then shift your attention to your
      torso, abdomen, lower back, upper back, chest, and shoulders. Go
      down each arm to your fingertips, and then move up the neck to
      all areas of your face. Finish at the top of your head.
   ♠ As you go through your body, there is no need to make anything
      special happen. Most of what you notice will be quite ordinary.
      You may notice itching, pressure, heaviness, stiffness, and so on. If
      you notice some pain, acknowledge it, and refocus on the body
      scan. The point of the exercise is to notice the sensations while
      keeping your attention on the body part of your focus.
   ♠ When you get to the top of your head, allow your attention to
      linger there for a few moments. Then start to notice your breath.
```

```text
Mindfulness of Routine Activities
You do not have to do formal exercises like those listed above to be
mindful. Instead you can practice being mindful during everyday activities.
For example, you can experience a mindful meal where you eat very
slowly and really pay attention to what you are eating. Engage all of your
senses in the process. Really smell your food and taste it. Notice the tex-
ture and temperature of it. If you are used to wolfing down your food,
you might find this a very pleasant experience.
    You can also have a mindful beverage. Whether it’s coffee, tea, wine,
or beer, take the time to slow down and be mindful of what you are
drinking. Pay special attention to really tasting the flavor. Notice the fra-
grance, the texture, and the temperature.
    Finally, you can be mindful during any of your daily activities. So often
we do things in such a routine, autopilot manner that we are going
through the motions in a very mindless way. When you pay attention to
your full experience, you are training your mind in a way that will improve
your ability to focus. Mindfulness has also been shown to improve mood
and boost immunity. The more mindful opportunities you create, the
more you will reap the benefits.
    As you may have figured out, the main reason to become more mindful
is to train yourself to reflect on and monitor your experiences objectively.
When you can step outside of yourself and be an objective observer,
you’ll be much more effective when you moderate and direct your behav-
ior. Being engaged like this is the precursor to playing in the zone, and
when you are in the zone, you will cease to be at the mercy of your
thoughts and emotions.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

Defuse Your Negative Thoughts
There is a school of psychology called Acceptance and Commitment
Training developed by Dr. Stephen Hayes, who has a compelling theory
about how the mind works to keep us off kilter, which he calls fusion.
When we are in a state of cognitive fusion, we’re inseparable from our
thoughts. We are so caught up in them that we allow them to dominate
our behavior. You get “pushed around” by your thoughts when you are in
this state. Your mind is like a dictator. The way I am using the term
“thoughts” here can include beliefs, assumptions, thoughts, attitudes,
memories, words, gestures, fantasies, and some aspects of emotions.
   Think about what happens when you let thoughts run your life. When
they dominate our attention, we get hooked in, and it’s easy to get car-
ried away with them. Being so caught up in our thoughts causes us to
miss out on many aspects of our here and now, and our thoughts have
such a huge impact on our behavior that our ability to act effectively is
significantly reduced.
   We are so caught up in all of those words and pictures running through
our heads, that we lose contact with the world of direct experience.
Mindfulness is a shuttle between these two worlds: it transports us from
the world of our thoughts to the world of direct experience.
   In a state of fusion, a thought can seem like:

   ♠ the absolute truth
   ♠ a command that you need to obey
   ♠ a threat that you need to get rid of as soon as possible
   ♠ something happening right here and now even though it happened
       in the past
   ♠ something very important that requires all of our attention
   ♠ something you can’t let go of even though it has a negative impact
       on your game (or your life).
```

```text
                                          Transform Your Mental Game

    Hayes uses the term “defusion” for the process of stepping back and
separating from or detaching from our thoughts, images, and memories.
If we defuse our negative thoughts we don’t get caught up in them or
pushed around by them but let them come and go as if they were clouds
in the sky. We step back and watch our thinking – almost as though we
were an observer. We see our thoughts for what they are: simply words
and pictures that may or may not be helpful.
    Once you are in a state of defusion, you can see the thought for what
it is: nothing more or less than a bunch of words or pictures inside your
head. Once you get to this point, you’ll realize that any given thought...

   ♠ may or may not be true
   ♠ is definitely not a command that you must obey
   ♠ is not a threat
   ♠ is not something happening in the physical world – it’s a mental
       representation in the form of words or images inside your head
   ♠ may or may not be important
   ♠ can be allowed to come and go of its own accord.

Practicing Thought Awareness
Here’s a quick exercise that you can use to develop your present moment
cognitive awareness:

   ♠ Close your eyes and notice what your mind does. Pay attention to
       what thoughts and images pop into your awareness. It may take a
       bit of time, but eventually you will be aware of something.
   ♠ Notice the tone of your thoughts. Are they negative or positive?
       Are there any images related to your thoughts? Do they seem to
       be located in any particular place in relation to you? Are they
       within you, or located outside of you?
```
